4 Part A — Collection and Pre-Processing

Before we can analyze data, we have to find it and clean it up.

4.1 1. Data Collection Strategies

Data collection is the process of gathering raw information from various sources to answer a specific business question.

It exists because algorithms cannot learn from nothing. You must feed them historical examples (data) so they can find patterns.

Tip🧠 Analogy — Mining for Gold

The everyday thing: A gold mining operation.

The mapping: - The mountain is the internet or your company’s user base. - The excavator is your data collection strategy (APIs, web scraping). - The chunks of raw rock you pull out are the raw data.

Where it breaks down: Mining removes gold from the mountain permanently, but collecting data from a website doesn’t delete the data from the website.

4.1.1 How it works

There are three primary ways modern teams collect data: 1. Internal Databases: Pulling data your company already owns (e.g., customer purchase history from a SQL database). 2. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces): Requesting data programmatically from third-party services (e.g., getting live weather data from the OpenWeather API). 3. Web Scraping: Writing scripts to automatically read and extract information from public websites when an API is not available.

4.1.2 ❓ MCQs

Q1. If you need to gather public pricing information from a competitor’s website that does not offer an API, which strategy must you use?

    1. Querying your internal SQL database.
    1. Web Scraping.
    1. Guessing the prices based on market trends.
    1. Waiting for the competitor to email you their data.
NoteAnswers

A1 — (b). Web scraping allows you to programmatically extract information directly from the HTML of a webpage when no official API is provided.

Once you collect the data, you will immediately notice a problem: it is never ready to use.

4.2 2. Data Pre-Processing Overview

Data pre-processing is the act of cleaning and formatting raw data into a pristine table that a machine learning algorithm can understand.

It exists because raw data is incredibly messy. Users make typos, sensors fail and record blank values, and different systems use different formats (e.g., 10/05/2024 vs 2024-10-05). If you feed messy data into a model, the model will produce garbage predictions.

Warning⚠️ The trap of skipping the cleaning phase

“I just want to get to the fun machine learning part!”

Garbage in, garbage out. If you don’t pre-process your data, your highly advanced neural network will confidently give you the wrong answer because it learned from typos and missing values. Data Scientists spend 80% of their time pre-processing.

4.2.1 How it works

Pre-processing generally involves: - Handling Missing Values: What do we do if a user didn’t enter their age? (Delete the row, or guess the average?) - Formatting: Ensuring all text is lowercase, or all dates follow the same format. - Removing Duplicates: Ensuring a user who clicked “Submit” twice isn’t counted as two separate purchases.

4.2.2 ❓ MCQs

Q2. Why do Data Scientists spend so much time pre-processing data?

    1. Because Python is very slow at reading files.
    1. Because raw data contains errors, missing values, and inconsistencies that ruin analysis.
    1. Because pre-processing is the only way to generate charts.
    1. Because it is required by international privacy laws.
NoteAnswers

A2 — (b). Real-world data is generated by humans and imperfect systems, leading to errors that must be fixed before an algorithm can find accurate patterns.

We know we need to collect and clean data, but what tool do we use to actually do this in Python?

5 Part B — Working with Pandas

Pandas is the industry-standard tool for looking at and manipulating tabular data in Python.

5.1 3. Working with Pandas data frames

A Pandas DataFrame is essentially a programmatic Excel spreadsheet inside Python.

It exists because standard Python lists and dictionaries are too slow and cumbersome for doing math on millions of rows of tabular data. Pandas gives us a fast, intuitive way to filter, group, and calculate statistics on large datasets.

5.1.1 How it works

You import the library (import pandas as pd), load a file (like a CSV) into a DataFrame object, and then use built-in methods to inspect it.

5.1.2 📘 Examples

Example 1 — Creating a simple DataFrame from scratch

import pandas as pd

# Creating data manually using a dictionary
data = {
    "Name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 35],
    "City": ["New York", "London", "Paris"]
}

# Converting it into a Pandas DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Displaying the DataFrame
df
Name Age City
0 Alice 25 New York
1 Bob 30 London
2 Charlie 35 Paris

Example 2 — Inspecting the data

# .head(2) shows only the first 2 rows. Useful when you have millions of rows!
df.head(2)

5.1.3 🌍 Scenarios

Scenario 1 — You have a massive file with 500,000 rows. You cannot print it to the screen. You must use df.head() to just peek at the first 5 rows to understand what the columns are.

6 Part Demo — Inspecting Messy Data

Loading a raw, messy dataset to inspect its structure using Pandas.

Let’s simulate loading a messy CSV file that a Data Engineer just handed to us. We will use three critical Pandas commands to figure out what is wrong with it: - .head() to look at the raw rows. - .info() to see data types and count missing values. - .describe() to see mathematical summaries.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Simulating a messy dataset being loaded from a CSV
messy_data = {
    "CustomerID": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
    "Age": [25, np.nan, 22, 150, 30], # Note the missing value (NaN) and the impossible age (150)
    "Income": [50000, 60000, np.nan, 120000, 45000],
    "Subscribed": ["Yes", "Y", "No", "N", "Yes"] # Inconsistent formatting
}

df_messy = pd.DataFrame(messy_data)

print("--- USING .head() ---")
# See the inconsistencies visually
display(df_messy.head())

print("\n--- USING .info() ---")
# See that Age and Income are missing some non-null values
df_messy.info()

print("\n--- USING .describe() ---")
# Notice that the max Age is 150! A clear error we need to fix later.
display(df_messy.describe())
